entities.summary:
Pál Tomori, born around 1475, was a Hungarian Franciscan friar who rose to become the Archbishop of Kalocsa and a pivotal military commander in the Kingdom of Hungary's desperate defense against the encroaching Ottoman Empire in the early 16th century. His career encapsulated the complex fusion of spiritual and temporal authority characteristic of late medieval Central Europe, culminating in his command at the catastrophic Battle of Mohács in 1526, a defeat that irrevocably altered the geopolitical landscape of the region. He embodied Hungary's last, valiant, but ultimately doomed, efforts to stem the Ottoman tide.

Initially a secular nobleman, Tomori renounced his worldly life after personal tragedy, joining the Franciscan Order and quickly gaining respect for his piety and administrative skills. Despite his monastic vows, King Louis II of Hungary, recognizing his strategic acumen and martial background, appointed him Archbishop of Kalocsa in 1523 and, crucially, tasked him with organizing the southern border defenses. In August 1523, Tomori achieved a significant, albeit temporary, victory by decisively defeating an Ottoman army at the Battle of Szávaszentdemeter (modern Sremska Mitrovica), earning him a reputation as a formidable frontier general. He was then made commander-in-chief of Hungary's southern forces, facing constant pressure and inadequate resources.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pál Tomori's leadership at the Battle of Mohács directly precipitated the collapse of the independent Kingdom of Hungary, leading to its partition and centuries of foreign rule. His actions and death significantly altered the political and religious landscape of Central Europe.
